title: From a travel idea to a trip that works
audience: Someone arriving from another field, with no assumed knowledge of travel businesses, accounting, or business software.
scope: An introduction to the work of tour operators and the software that connects planning, sales, suppliers, travellers, and finance. Examples reflect group and tailor-made travel in a European setting. Legal duties depend on the arrangement, country, and applicable dates. This is not a guide to running an airline or choosing a holiday. Nora, Coast & Village Travel, the trip, and all prices and contract terms are fictional.
learningGoals: Explain how a tour operator combines services into one trip, and where its software fits.
Distinguish a travel product, a departure, a booking, and a supplier confirmation.
Follow a trip through preparation, a disruption, delivery, and financial checks.
Explain why availability, profit, cash, and traveller confidence need separate attention.

introduction.whatItIs: Imagine arranging a weekend away for friends. The dates must work, beds must be available, transport must arrive, and everyone needs the right instructions. A tour operator does this professionally, often coordinating services supplied by several other businesses. Some sell scheduled group trips; others build a different itinerary for each customer.
introduction.whyItMatters: The visible product is a holiday description and a booking button. Behind it are promises, supplier requests, traveller details, bills, and decisions about changes. Tour operator ERP software connects this work. ERP means enterprise resource planning: here, shared business records and workflows linking the trip being sold to the services and money behind it.
introduction.familiarComparison: Think of organizing a wedding using an independent venue, caterer, photographer, and transport company. Each supplier can do its own job well, yet the event still needs someone to coordinate the whole.
introduction.whereComparisonBreaks: Travel businesses may coordinate many departures at once, sell through other agents, and support people far from home. Package-travel rules can also place responsibilities on the organizer. The software provider supplies tools; the travel business makes and manages the travel arrangements.

participants.name: Travellers
participants.role: Choose and pay for a trip, provide needed details, and experience the result. The person booking may be arranging travel for several people.
participants.caresAbout: An accurate description, a workable trip, clear terms, and timely help when something changes.

participants.name: The tour operator
participants.role: Designs trips, agrees supplier terms, sells places, coordinates delivery, and manages the finances. Nora is a trip planner at fictional Coast & Village Travel.
participants.caresAbout: Keeping promises while covering costs. Sales, operations, service, and finance colleagues need compatible versions of the same information.

participants.name: Suppliers and destination partners
participants.role: Provide accommodation, transport, guiding, or activities. A destination management company is a local business that can coordinate several such services for the operator.
participants.caresAbout: Clear requests, realistic timings, confirmed quantities, and payment under the agreed terms.

participants.name: Travel agents and other resellers
participants.role: Help customers choose and book travel supplied by another business. Their exact commercial and legal role depends on the arrangement.
participants.caresAbout: Reliable availability, clear booking status, and any commission: a fee earned for selling the trip.

participants.name: The software provider
participants.role: Supplies and supports the business system, websites, or portals. The travel organization pays for access and often for setup or additional services.
participants.caresAbout: Reliable workflows, usable connections to other systems, and customers who can operate the software confidently. It does not own the hotel rooms or deliver the holiday.

participantsOverview.illustrationPrompt: An adult teaching map about coordination, not money or ownership. Center a woman at a desk labeled 'Tour operator'. Around her four separate cards: travellers with luggage labeled 'Travellers'; hotel, minibus and guide labeled 'Suppliers and local partners'; person at travel desk labeled 'Travel agents'; laptop support person labeled 'Software provider'. Exactly four connections, each ONLY between the center and one card. Traveller connection label 'Plans and updates'; supplier connection label 'Requests and confirmations'; agent connection label 'Booking details'; software connection label 'Tools and support'. Use plain lines without arrowheads: these describe coordination relationships, not a complete delivery route. No links between outside cards. No money, prices, ownership symbols or decorative extra words. Large legible labels, warm white, navy, teal and restrained amber.

media.title: Who coordinates and delivers the trip
media.alt: The tour operator coordinates plans and updates with travellers, requests and confirmations with suppliers and local partners, booking details with agents, and tools and support with the software provider.
media.caption: The map shows coordination relationships. Suppliers deliver the travel services, while the software provider supports the travel business.

concepts.meaning: A component is one travel service, such as a hotel stay or a guided walk. An operator combines components into an offer. A package has a specific legal meaning; under EU rules, certain combinations of different travel-service types qualify, depending on how they are offered and booked.
concepts.example: Nora combines minibus travel, two nights at a hotel, and a guided walk. She needs to know both what the customer is buying and which business must arrange each part.
concepts.whyItMatters: Customers experience the connected trip. A lovely hotel does not solve a missing transfer. Legal classification also affects the organizer's obligations.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Three large service cards on the left labeled 'Transport', 'Stay', 'Guided walk', showing a minibus, a hotel bed, and a guide beside a coastal path. One bracket gathers them toward a single large trip folder on the right labeled 'One coordinated trip'. Footer label 'Each part must work'. Show a human planner beside the folder. Exactly these five labels. No equals sign, legal seal, automatic booking check, prices or claim that every combination legally qualifies as a package. Adult simple navy teal amber illustration on warm white.

media.title: Travel components and packages
media.alt: Transport, a hotel stay, and a guided walk are gathered into one trip folder beside a planner.
media.caption: The operator connects separate services into an experience whose parts must work together. Legal package classification depends on the actual arrangement.

concepts.term: A travel product and a departure
concepts.meaning: The product describes the trip being offered. A departure is a particular run of that trip on particular dates. Each departure has its own capacity, bookings, supplier arrangements, and outcome.
concepts.example: Coast & Village Weekend is the product. Its September and October departures may follow the same route but use different guides or have different numbers of travellers.
concepts.whyItMatters: A good description can be reused; availability cannot simply be copied from one departure to another. A tailor-made trip may instead have one customer-specific set of dates and services.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: One top card labeled 'Travel product' contains a simple coast-and-village route and minibus icon. It branches into two equally sized separate calendar cards below, labeled 'September departure' and 'October departure'. Each lower card has its own small group of traveller icons and separate hotel/guide icons. No numbered dates, amounts, capacity counts or arrows between the two departures. Exactly three text labels. The route concept is shared while the dated arrangements remain separate. Clear adult editorial design.

media.title: A travel product and a departure
media.alt: One coastal travel product branches into separate September and October departures, each with its own travellers, hotel, and guide.
media.caption: The trip idea can be shared while each departure keeps its own dates, capacity, bookings, and supplier arrangements.

concepts.meaning: Availability means the required services can be supplied for the right dates and people. An allotment is a quantity a supplier makes available under an agreement. A release date is an agreed point when unused capacity may return to the supplier. Payment and cancellation commitments depend on that agreement.
concepts.example: Nora needs three twin rooms on each of two nights for six travellers who agree to share. Six minibus passenger places do not help if only two suitable rooms are available on the second night.
concepts.whyItMatters: Rooms, beds, seats, dates, and room-sharing arrangements are different things. Holding capacity can improve certainty while creating deadlines or financial exposure.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Two-panel availability lesson. Left panel labeled 'Transport' shows a minibus with label '6 traveller places'. Right panel labeled 'Hotel rooms' shows a simple two-row table: 'Night 1' with three twin-bed room icons, and 'Night 2' with two twin-bed room icons and one amber empty outlined slot with a question mark. Footer 'Check every required service and date'. No green overall confirmation, no money, no passenger-name text, no calendar dates beyond Night 1 and Night 2. Keep room icons clear: each occupied room icon has TWO single beds. Large typography and simple shapes.

media.title: Availability, allotments, and release dates
media.alt: A minibus has six traveller places. A hotel grid has three twin rooms for night one but only two for night two, with a question mark in the remaining slot.
media.caption: The planned six-person trip needs suitable capacity for every service and date. Available seats do not make up for a missing room.

concepts.meaning: A quote describes an offer and its terms. A booking records the customer's arrangement with the seller. Supplier confirmation records a supplier's agreement to provide a particular service. Systems track both the overall booking and the individual services; the labels and contract effects depend on the business process.
concepts.example: A traveller accepts Nora's offer, while the hotel request is still awaiting a reply. That customer action does not itself make the hotel rooms confirmed.
concepts.whyItMatters: An overall status can hide an unresolved component. The team must communicate accurately and avoid promises that the supplier arrangements cannot support.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: Left card shows customer accepting an offer, labeled 'Customer booking'. To the right are two completely separate supplier cards: a minibus labeled 'Transport confirmed' with a small teal tick; a hotel labeled 'Hotel awaiting reply' with an amber clock. Under all cards a question 'Are all services secured?'. No overall green check, no arrow automatically turning the hotel green, no payment icons, no invented dates or numbers. Exactly these four labels. Adult learning diagram with generous spacing.

media.title: Quote, booking, and supplier confirmation
media.alt: A customer accepts a booking while separate service cards show transport confirmed and the hotel still awaiting a reply.
media.caption: Check customer arrangements and supplier commitments separately. One confirmed service does not confirm the whole trip.

concepts.meaning: An itinerary tells travellers what happens when and where. Operational lists tell the people delivering the trip what they need to do: for example, a rooming list assigns guests to room arrangements, while a pickup list helps a driver collect the right people.
concepts.example: Travellers need the hotel address and meeting time. The hotel needs agreed room arrangements. The guide needs the group schedule and relevant requirements.
concepts.whyItMatters: Different people need different views of consistent information. Sharing every traveller detail with everyone creates confusion and unnecessary privacy exposure.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: One central trip folder labeled 'Shared trip details' feeds three distinct simple documents, with arrows pointing outward. Document 1 labeled 'Traveller itinerary' has route and clock icons. Document 2 labeled 'Hotel rooming list' has twin-bed icons. Document 3 labeled 'Driver pickup list' has minibus and map-pin icons. No names, passport numbers, diagnoses, financial data, or extra text anywhere on documents; use abstract lines. Exactly four labels. Each document is next to the relevant traveller, hotel worker, or driver.

media.title: The itinerary and operational lists
media.alt: Shared trip details feed a traveller itinerary, a hotel rooming list, and a driver pickup list.
media.caption: Different views should agree on the underlying trip while giving each recipient only the information needed for their role.

concepts.term: Sales, direct costs, and trip margin
concepts.meaning: Sales are the amounts charged to customers for the trip. Direct costs are costs assigned to delivering it, such as the hotel, transport, and guide. In this guide, trip margin means sales minus those direct costs. It still has to help cover office salaries, software, marketing, and other costs.
concepts.example: Six travellers paying €150 produce €900 of sales. The minibus costs €300, hotel €300, and guide €100: €700 in direct costs. The trip margin is €200. All figures are illustrative and exclude taxes and other costs.
concepts.whyItMatters: A busy departure is not automatically profitable. Some costs stay much the same when fewer people travel; others change with the number of people or rooms.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: An extremely clear financial teaching diagram. One long top bar labeled 'Sales €900'. Beneath it a matching total-width bar divided into 'Direct costs €700' and 'Trip margin €200', with lengths approximately seven-ninths and two-ninths. Under the cost part three simple icons with labels 'Transport €300', 'Hotel €300', 'Guide €100'. Small footer 'Before taxes and other costs'. ONLY these seven labels, no percentages, no net profit label, no growing coins, no extra arithmetic. Navy costs and teal margin, warm white background. This is a fictional six-traveller example.

media.title: Sales, direct costs, and trip margin
media.alt: Sales of €900 split into €700 of direct costs and €200 of trip margin. The costs comprise transport €300, hotel €300, and guide €100.
media.caption: This fictional calculation leaves €200 before the other costs and taxes excluded from the example.

concepts.meaning: Cash timing concerns when money actually arrives and leaves. A deposit is an advance payment, not necessarily the whole price. Settlement means checking and completing amounts owed. Reconciliation means matching records, such as a bank receipt to the booking it pays for.
concepts.example: The six travellers pay €45 deposits, bringing in €270. Suppose supplier advances of €350 are due before the remaining customer payments. The operator must plan the €80 timing gap, even though the trip is expected to have a positive margin.
concepts.whyItMatters: Expected margin does not pay a bill today. Finance must also follow applicable rules for protecting customer money and handle refunds or disputed amounts correctly.
concepts.illustrationPrompt: A simple two-stage timeline about payment timing. First stage heading 'Now' has two separate cards labeled 'Customer deposits €270' and 'Supplier advances €350'. Beneath them an amber bracket labeled 'Timing gap €80'. Second stage heading 'Later' has a customer payment envelope labeled 'Remaining customer payments'. One neutral time arrow from Now to Later. Do not depict customer cash being automatically forwarded, do not add balances, dates, percentages or lending advice, and do not label the gap a loss. Exactly these six labels. Clean adult diagram.

media.title: Cash timing and settlement
media.alt: Customer deposits of €270 and supplier advances of €350 create an €80 timing gap now; remaining customer payments arrive later.
media.caption: Payment dates create a cash-planning problem even when the expected trip margin is positive.

historyNote: These British, American, and EU examples explain parts of today's travel business. They are selected milestones, not a claim that one company invented organized travel or that all countries developed in the same way.

history.change: Thomas Cook organized a rail excursion from Leicester to Loughborough. It is a well-known example of arranging travel for a group before modern booking systems.
history.whyItMatters: The coordination job is older than the software: connecting people, transport, timing, and an understandable offer.

history.change: American Airlines and IBM's Sabre system connected reservation offices to centralized flight information and booking processing.
history.whyItMatters: This airline example shows why shared availability and reservation records matter when many people sell limited capacity. A tour still requires coordination beyond an airline reservation.

history.period: 2015 onward: rules adapt to assembled travel
history.change: The EU's 2015 Package Travel Directive addressed both pre-arranged holidays and certain trips assembled through newer booking processes. It was amended in 2026.
history.whyItMatters: How a trip is offered and bought can affect responsibilities. Teams need to check the rules and application dates relevant to their arrangements.

walkthrough.title: Nora organizes a six-person weekend
walkthrough.setup: This fictional three-day trip includes minibus travel, two hotel nights, and a guided walk. Six adults agree to share three twin rooms. The €150 price per person and all supplier amounts are teaching figures, not real travel prices. Assume taxes and other costs are excluded throughout the example.

steps.title: Describe the trip and who it suits
steps.whatHappens: Nora records the route, dates, inclusions, room arrangements, meeting points, and practical requirements. She makes the offer clear enough for travellers to judge whether it suits them.
steps.whyItMatters: Good preparation starts with a trip people can actually take, including any relevant access or mobility requirements.

steps.title: Arrange supply and calculate the offer
steps.whatHappens: She checks suitable transport, three twin rooms for both nights, and a guide. She records supplier terms and deadlines. Expected direct costs are €700 against €900 sales if all six places sell.
steps.whyItMatters: Capacity, price, and commitments must fit the same departure. Nora also considers the effect of selling fewer places.

steps.title: Record bookings and confirm each component
steps.whatHappens: The six travellers accept the offer. Nora records their arrangements and supplier replies, resolving pending items before treating the trip as secured. Finance matches €270 of customer deposits to bookings and plans the €350 of supplier advances.
steps.whyItMatters: Customer commitments, supplier commitments, and payments remain visible as distinct facts.

steps.title: Prepare the people delivering the trip
steps.whatHappens: Nora checks guest details and agreed room sharing, then prepares itineraries, rooming information, pickup details, and guide instructions. Each recipient gets the information needed for their role.
steps.whyItMatters: A confirmed hotel still needs to know whom to expect. Preparing different documents from shared records reduces contradictions.

steps.title: Handle a hotel problem
steps.whatHappens: The hotel can no longer provide the rooms. Nora finds a suitable alternative, explains the change and available options, and checks the applicable obligations. In this case all travellers accept, and the operator keeps their price unchanged.
steps.whyItMatters: Assume the original hotel payment is fully refunded and the replacement costs €360. Direct costs rise to €760, leaving €140 trip margin.
steps.watchOut: Nora updates the hotel details, rooming instructions, driver destination, guide plan, customer itinerary, and financial records. Changing only the customer email would leave other people working from the old plan.

steps.title: Deliver, check, and close the trip
steps.whatHappens: The group travels and the team handles any questions. Afterwards, finance matches final supplier bills, refunds, and customer payments to the records. Nora reviews traveller feedback and the departure's actual costs.
steps.whyItMatters: The group returning home and the accounts being settled are separate milestones. Actual results inform the next departure.

walkthrough.outcome: The travellers complete the agreed trip with the replacement hotel. Everyone delivering it receives the updated plan, and the operator can explain the €140 margin before other costs. The software supports these handoffs; Nora and her colleagues make and check the decisions.
walkthrough.illustrationPrompt: A spare six-panel editorial storyboard with only SIX text labels. Strict 3-column by 2-row grid; one large title per panel: '1 Plan', '2 Arrange supply', '3 Confirm', '4 Prepare', '5 Handle change', '6 Deliver and settle'. Absolutely no other words, letters, names, dates, amounts or numbers anywhere: screens and documents contain only abstract lines, colored shapes and icons. No lists of passenger names. No captions inside panels. Consistent Nora has short curly dark hair and a teal jacket. 1: Nora and travellers examine a coastal route. 2: Nora considers separate hotel, minibus and walking-guide picture cards. 3: Nora checks two separate piles of customer and supplier documents, with simple person and hotel icons. 4: Nora gives different documents to a hotel worker and minibus driver. 5: Nora phones while replacing an unavailable hotel picture with another, simple amber question mark. 6: travellers enjoy the coastal village, with a separate small finance scene of a person matching paper records. Use big human scenes and white space, not dense process diagrams. No arrows between panels. All six headings must be very legible at thumbnail size.

media.title: Nora takes the trip from plan to settlement
media.alt: Six scenes show Nora planning the trip, arranging supply, checking confirmations, preparing instructions, handling a hotel change, and supporting delivery and financial settlement.
media.caption: A hotel change affects the whole trip. Nora updates the people, documents, and financial records before the group travels.

valueAndIncentives.title: The traveller buys coordination
valueAndIncentives.explanation: The benefit is a useful whole: a suitable trip, manageable arrangements, and a contact when something changes. Combining services adds work as well as convenience.
valueAndIncentives.example: Nora's hotel replacement protects the trip because she also changes transport and joining instructions.

valueAndIncentives.title: The travel business and software business earn differently
valueAndIncentives.explanation: The operator receives travel sales and pays suppliers and operating costs. An agent may earn commission. The software provider receives fees for the system, implementation, support, or additional services.
valueAndIncentives.example: The €900 trip sale is the operator's transaction. It is not €900 of revenue for its software supplier.

valueAndIncentives.title: Reliable operations need resources
valueAndIncentives.explanation: Supplier relationships, knowledgeable staff, accurate records, and disruption handling cost time and money. Faster quoting is useful when the resulting offer remains deliverable.
valueAndIncentives.example: A sales team rewarded only for booking volume may overlook expensive changes that appear later in the departure's accounts.

challenges.title: Promising capacity that several businesses control
challenges.whyHard: A supplier can change availability while requests move between people and systems. The trip needs its components to fit together.
challenges.tradeOff: Holding more capacity improves certainty but may create commitments or release deadlines.
challenges.example: Six seats are available while a hotel has too few rooms for the agreed sharing arrangements.
challenges.commonApproach: Track service-level confirmation and deadlines, check important replies, and keep useful alternatives. An online connection helps only when its data and booking responses are reliable.

challenges.title: Making each trip personal without losing control
challenges.whyHard: A room change, access requirement, or extra activity can affect prices, capacity, documents, and supplier instructions.
challenges.tradeOff: More choice helps customers but increases the combinations the team must check.
challenges.example: A traveller requests a room alone after the original plan assumed sharing.
challenges.commonApproach: Record the request once, examine its effects, and confirm the agreed change with the affected parties. A prettier itinerary cannot resolve an unavailable room.

challenges.title: Keeping departures financially viable
challenges.whyHard: Some supplier costs remain even when fewer people book. Seasonality and advance payments can add pressure.
challenges.tradeOff: An attractive price can increase demand while leaving less room to handle disruption.
challenges.example: The replacement hotel reduces Nora's expected €200 margin to €140.
challenges.commonApproach: Review costs at different group sizes and update forecasts as commitments change. Track cash dates separately; neither a sales total nor an expected margin gives the whole picture.

challenges.title: Helping travellers during a disruption
challenges.whyHard: Time is short, several parties may be affected, and the operator must understand its obligations as well as the practical alternatives.
challenges.tradeOff: A quick fix may cost more; a slow decision can leave people uncertain or stranded.
challenges.example: A replacement hotel is useful only if it fits the travellers' needs and everyone receives the new instructions.
challenges.commonApproach: Assign a decision-maker, keep contact and commitment records accessible, and communicate clear options. Automation can distribute an update, but cannot judge every alternative's suitability.

challenges.title: Sharing accurate information with the right people
challenges.whyHard: Travellers, agents, hotels, and guides need different details. Old versions and unnecessary personal data can spread easily.
challenges.tradeOff: Easy access supports delivery; indiscriminate sharing creates confusion and privacy exposure.
challenges.example: A driver needs pickup information, not the operator's complete customer file.
challenges.commonApproach: Use role-appropriate views, version important documents, and review sensitive requests. A shared system helps only if people maintain the records and use the current version.

misconceptions.belief: A booking button means every component is confirmed.
misconceptions.reality: The process may still contain supplier requests or conditions. Check the actual arrangement and individual service statuses.

misconceptions.belief: A room, a bed, and a place on the trip are interchangeable.
misconceptions.reality: Capacity must fit dates, people, and agreed arrangements. One available room does not automatically satisfy any two travellers.
They are cash received towards a booking. Supplier obligations, remaining payments, refunds, and other costs still need attention.

misconceptions.belief: The software organizes and delivers the holiday by itself.
misconceptions.reality: It connects records and supports repeatable work. People and suppliers still arrange, deliver, and resolve the trip.

takeaways: The operator coordinates a whole trip from services delivered by several parties.
Products, departures, customer bookings, and supplier confirmations describe different things.
Changing one component can change many people's instructions and the trip's economics.
Successful delivery, financial settlement, and useful feedback all matter after the sale.

knowledgeChecks.question: A customer accepts the offer and the minibus is confirmed, but the hotel has not replied. Is the complete trip secured?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. The hotel remains an unresolved component that must be handled and communicated accurately.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: The customer's booking and each supplier's commitment are separate facts.

knowledgeChecks.question: There are six passenger places but only two twin rooms available on the second night. Can Nora promise the planned arrangements for all six travellers?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. The plan needs three twin rooms on each night, assuming the agreed sharing arrangement.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Availability must work across all required services and dates; sufficient transport alone does not settle it.

knowledgeChecks.question: The trip sells for €900 and the replacement raises direct costs to €760. Is the remaining €140 the business's final profit?
knowledgeChecks.answer: No. It is the trip margin as defined here, before the other costs and taxes excluded from this example.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Office staff, software, marketing, and other expenses still have to be covered.

knowledgeChecks.question: Customer deposits of €270 have arrived and €350 of supplier advances are due. What does finance need to notice?
knowledgeChecks.answer: An €80 timing gap, along with any rules governing how customer money is held and used.
knowledgeChecks.explanation: A positive expected trip margin does not mean enough cash is available at every payment date.
